summary: Specifies how to carry audio from the G.719 full-band codec in RTP, including multiple channels, multiple frames per packet, and interleaving. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: This explains how to pack sound in one audio format into small packages for sending over the Internet, even with several channels at once.

subtitle: How to pack G.719 full-band audio into RTP packets, with multiple channels, several frames per packet and optional interleaving.

tldr.problem: G.719 is a codec that encodes audio at 32 to 128 kbit/s in 20-ms frames, but it needs a defined way to ride inside RTP packets, carry several channels, and survive packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload starts with table of contents (ToC) entries that give frame length and count, followed by the audio frames. An optional interleaved mode adds displacement fields so consecutive frames are spread over different packets.
tldr.outcome: The payload format is a Proposed Standard. Basic mode must be implemented and interleaved mode should be, and the media type audio/G719 is registered for it.

today: RFC 5404 is a Proposed Standard, and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5404 specifies how audio from the ITU-T G.719 full-band (FB) codec is packetized into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP, RFC 3550). The format supports transmission of multiple channels, multiple frames per payload, and packet loss robustness through redundancy or interleaving.

The document describes the codec and the format's capabilities, defines the payload in Section 5, gives examples, and then specifies the media type, its mapping to the Session Description Protocol (SDP) and its use in SDP offer/answer. It ends with congestion control and security.

A key term is the frame-block: in an N-channel session, the set of N audio frames, one per channel, that represent exactly the same time period.
sections.eli5: A special kind of sound recording needs a standard way to be put into Internet packages. This document is the packing instructions, including how to pack stereo sound where the left and right parts travel together.

sections.title: The G.719 Codec
sections.content:
G.719 is a low-complexity transform coder based on the Modulated Lapped Transform (MLT). Its input and output are sampled at 48 kHz, it covers 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and it encodes speech, music and general audio at rates from 32 kbit/s up to 128 kbit/s. It works on 20-ms frames and has an algorithmic delay of 40 ms. The bitrate can change at any 20-ms frame boundary.

For each frame the encoder chooses between a stationary mode, with a long MLT giving a spectrum of 960 coefficients, and a transient mode, with a short MLT giving 4 spectra of 240 coefficients. Only the spectral envelope is transmitted, and the decoder repeats the bit allocation. Coefficients that received no bits are replaced by entries from a noise codebook built from the decoded coefficients.

Other sampling rates are possible by resampling to 48 kHz, but this is not part of the standard.
sections.eli5: The codec chops sound into tiny 20-millisecond slices and describes each slice compactly. If a slice has details that were skipped, the decoder fills in a bit of quiet noise so it does not sound empty.

sections.title: What the Payload Format Can Do
sections.content:
Rate adaptation. G.719 can change its encoding rate for each frame, which supports bitrate adaptation and congestion control. Putting more frames into one RTP payload lowers overhead, at the cost of more delay and less loss robustness.

Multiple channels. G.719 cannot encode multi-channel audio into one bit stream, but each channel can be encoded separately. The frames for all channels covering the same 20-ms period form a frame-block. The channel count is signaled out of band, and the channel order follows Section 4.1 of RFC 3551.

Redundancy. Generic FEC (RFC 5109) and audio redundancy coding (RFC 2198) can be used. This memo adds a G.719-specific form: earlier frames are aggregated with new ones, for example in a sliding window, and NO_DATA frames can fill gaps. The cost is bandwidth and receiver delay. The sender picks the amount of redundancy using feedback such as RTCP receiver reports.

Interleaving. Bundling frames means a lost packet loses consecutive frames, which is hard to conceal. Interleaving spreads those losses into isolated frame losses, but increases delay and buffering, so it suits streaming more than conversation. Its use must be negotiated at session setup. In the RFC's constant-delay example each packet carries two frames and the de-interleaving buffer needs room for at least three frames.
sections.eli5: You can send two or more slices of sound in one package to save postage. To protect against a lost package you can send copies, or mix up the order so that a lost package only takes away scattered tiny bits instead of one long gap.

sections.title: The Payload Structure and ToC
sections.content:
The RTP timestamp clock frequency SHALL be 48000 Hz, and the timestamp refers to the first sample of the first frame-block. The marker bit is set to 1 when the first frame-block is the first in a talkspurt, and 0 otherwise. The payload type is bound dynamically, because it expresses the configuration (basic or interleaved mode, and the number of channels).

A payload is one or more table of contents (ToC) entries followed by the audio data. Each basic ToC element is one byte: F (1 bit, set to 1 if another ToC entry follows), L (5 bits, frame length code) and two reserved bits, which SHALL be zero on sending and ignored on reception.

The L value maps to a frame length: 0 is NO_DATA, 8 to 22 give 80+10*(L-8) bytes, 23 to 27 give 240+20*(L-23) bytes, and 1 to 7 and 28 to 31 are reserved. A packet with a reserved value SHOULD be treated as invalid and discarded. For example L=8 is 80 bytes (32 kbps) and L=27 is 320 bytes (128 kbps).

In basic mode the basic ToC byte is followed by a one-octet #frames field, the number of frame-blocks of that length. In interleaved mode it is followed by #frames and then one 4-bit displacement field (DIS) per frame-block, giving the distance in 20-ms frame-blocks from the preceding one, with values 0 to 15. The first DIS of the payload is meaningless: it SHALL be zero and be ignored. A 4-bit pad is added when the group has an odd number of frame-blocks.

The audio data follows the ToC. Frame-blocks are packed oldest first, and within a frame-block the channels are concatenated in the RFC 3551 order. A receiver SHOULD discard a packet whose size does not match its ToC.
sections.eli5: Every package starts with a little contents list saying how big each slice of sound is and how many there are. If the package is in shuffle mode, the list also says how far apart in time the slices really were.

sections.title: Worked Payload Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three bit-level examples. The first is three mono frames at two bitrates: two frames of 80 bytes (32 kbps) and one of 120 bytes (48 kbps), using two ToC entries. The first has F=1, L=01000 and #frames=2, and the second has F=0, L=01100 and #frames=1.

The second is two stereo frame-blocks of 80 bytes per channel. The receiver multiplies the channels parameter (2) by the #frames value (2) to get 4 audio frames in the payload.

The third is four interleaved mono frames of 80 bytes. Packet n carries frame-blocks 13, 18, 23 and 28, with DIS1 equal to 0 and DIS2 to DIS4 each equal to 4.
sections.eli5: The examples show real contents lists for a few packages: one with slices of two sizes, one with left and right sound together, and one with slices picked from far-apart moments.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters and SDP
sections.content:
The format uses the media type audio/G719, registered in the IETF tree. Unspecified parameters MUST be ignored by the receiver. The optional parameters are:

  • interleaving: if present, interleaved mode is used, and the value is the number of frame-block slots in the de-interleaving buffer. It MUST be greater than zero. Without it, interleaved mode SHALL NOT be used.
  • int-delay: minimal media time in milliseconds the buffer needs before decoding starts, per SSRC, from zero to 65535.
  • max-red: the maximum time in milliseconds between a frame's first transmission and any redundant copy. Zero means no redundancy.
  • channels: 1 to 6, default 1.
  • CBR: the exact codec bitrate in bits per second, for cases where a variable rate cannot be supported, such as a gateway to H.320.
  • ptime and maxptime, as in RFC 4566.

In SDP, the RTP clock rate in a=rtpmap MUST be 48000, and the other parameters go in a=fmtp. In offer/answer (RFC 3264), the answerer MUST return interleaving and channels unmodified, although the value of interleaving MAY change. An offerer that wants interleaving or more than one channel is RECOMMENDED to also offer a single-channel payload type. With no b= line, a rate up to 128 kbps is implied. In declarative SDP, such as in RTSP or SAP, the configuration parameters are declarative and a participant MUST use what is given.
sections.eli5: Before a call, both sides swap a short settings card: how many channels, whether shuffle mode is allowed, and how much waiting room they have. The answer has to agree with the card for the important settings.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
General RTP congestion control applies (RFC 3550, RFC 3551), and the multi-rate feature of G.719 helps because the bitrate can be lowered. Packing more frames per payload reduces header overhead but adds delay and reduces robustness. A sender SHALL NOT increase its total bitrate when adding redundancy in response to loss, so the media bitrate must be reduced to make room.

The CBR parameter locks a payload type to one rate, which limits congestion response. Implementations SHOULD NOT use it unless talking to a device that cannot do variable bitrate, and a receiver in CBR mode MUST monitor the packet loss rate.

Basic mode SHALL be implemented and interleaved mode SHOULD be. Receiving redundant frames MUST be supported, and when copies arrive at different bitrates for one time slot, keeping the highest bitrate is RECOMMENDED. When interleaving, decoding may start once at least two consecutive frames are available and at least half of the frames in the planned period have arrived.
sections.eli5: If the road is jammed, the sender should send smaller packages, not more. Sending extra copies must never make the jam worse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concerns are confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. The RFC recommends SRTP (RFC 3711) where suitable, and mentions IPsec and TLS as alternatives.

Interleaving can weaken confidentiality for a short time after a key change. If a key is changed at timestamp 16, frames sent earlier under the old key may still be received and, with error concealment, could make some later audio intelligible. The RFC therefore recommends that interleaving patterns not overlap key changes when some clients lack a key.

The format has no significant non-uniform decoding complexity, so pathological data is unlikely to be a denial-of-service threat, and it contains no active content.
sections.eli5: Locks protect the sound from eavesdroppers. But if packages were shuffled, some pieces sent before you changed the lock can still reach someone who should not hear the later part.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: 1 if another ToC entry follows, 0 if this is the last.

fields.desc: Frame length code for each frame in the frame-block.

fields.desc: Reserved; zero on sending, ignored on reception.
